I have been farming here in Quzhou for over thirty years. My family has 5 mu of flat land near the village, good soil but getting drier every year. My husband works part-time at a construction site in Handan now, so most of the farm work falls on me. I never went to school, but I know this land — when to sow, when to water, and which seeds work.

This year, like every year, I will grow **winter wheat** and **summer maize** in rotation. It is the middle of April, and my wheat is already thick and green in the field — I sowed it last October after the National Day holiday. Wheat and maize are the only crops I trust. My neighbors who tried cotton last year spent too much money on pesticide and their backs ached from spraying every week. I am fifty now; I cannot bend down like that anymore. Wheat and maize give me grain for our own flour and cooking oil, and I can sell the extra to the grain buyer who drives his truck to the village edge.

For the **wheat**, I have 5 mu. I use improved seeds — I bought *Lüyuán 502* from the seed station last autumn because it resists lodging and the yield is steady. Before sowing, I hired the rotary tiller to break up the wheat stubble from the previous year. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer at sowing, and I will topdress with urea when the wheat starts jointing in late April. I irrigate three times: once now in spring, once when the heads come out, and once when the grains are filling. I spray pesticide about four times — mainly for aphids and the occasional rust — but I watch the fields first. If the pests are not bad, I skip a spray and save the money.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant **summer maize** on the same 5 mu. Time is short — if I wait too long, the frost in October will catch me. I buy hybrid seed, *Denghai 605*, because it grows fast and yields well even if the summer is a bit dry. I do not till the soil for maize — I plant directly into the wheat stubble with the no-till planter. This saves me labor and keeps the moisture in the ground. I put compound fertilizer in the planting furrow, and if the plants look yellow after the rain, I spread a little urea at the knee-high stage. I irrigate twice: once when the tassels appear, and once during grain filling. For pests, I spray two or three times — usually herbicide once right after sowing, and insecticide once or twice if the corn borer shows up.

I thought about renting another 2 mu, but the rent is too high this year, and fertilizer prices have gone up. Five mu of wheat and five mu of maize is enough for our family. I expect about 1,000 jin of wheat per mu and a bit more than 1,000 jin of maize per mu. If the drought does not get worse, I should have grain left over to sell.
